shots.text: Later, archaeologists from Goethe University Frankfurt went looking.
shots.desc: 4x4 on a dirt track through the plateau, dust

shots.text: All of the team's first thirty sites had been looted.
shots.desc: field of abandoned looters' pits, spoil heaps, grass regrowing

shots.text: In their key study area, plundered sites dominate.
shots.desc: aerial view of pitted ground among farmland

shots.text: Forgeries became a known problem too.
Today, Nok terracottas are on the International Council of Museums' Red List of objects at risk.
shots.desc: empty museum plinth under a spotlight

shots.text: Very few Nok figures come from recorded excavations, and complete ones are extremely rare.
shots.desc: a single clay fragment on a sieve, soil falling through

shots.text: That loss makes even a simple question hard. When?
shots.desc: soil section with charcoal lenses, side light

shots.text: Britannica still describes Nok as existing between about 500 BCE and 200 CE.
That range came from a handful of early radiocarbon and thermoluminescence dates.
shots.desc: old laboratory bench, glassware, sample tins

shots.text: Museum records vary too: the Cleveland Museum of Art gives this head a thermoluminescence date of 20 to 620 CE.
